docs.title: Course work for 113475 Software Defined Infrastructure
docs.text: This documentation is meant to supplement the submitted code for the Software defined Infrastructure lecture exercises.

docs.title: Exercise solutions
docs.text:
All solutions are documented and can be navigated to via the sidebar to the left. There is a page for each exercise, containing entries which detail the exercise description, document the implemented solution, and a verification of the intended results.

Before viewing the solutions, it is advisable to read through the Preliminaries section. It contains information that details how to set up the project files to replicate the results with the provided solutions.

The task pages log the exercise descriptions as well as the introduced topics. The solution pages have been written in a matter that can be followed along, while the result pages document the exercise results during creation of the submissions. If exercises build on each other, previous solution approaches are presumed to be known and won't be rehashed in detail for each individual exercise.

Solutions were produced on OS X. Operating System differences may lead to solutions not working right out of the box without adjustments (e.g. differences in file path semantics, etc.).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
To follow the solutions provided, please ensure the following prerequisites are met:

  • Generating SSH Key-Pair
  • Install Terraform
  • Hetzner Signup
  • Generating an API Token

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text: To facilitate more efficient interaction with the CLI tools used when creating cloud infrastructure, some aliases have been created. These are documented here in case they show up in screenshots of the conducted steps:

docs.title: SSHDM
docs.text:
alias sshdm="ssh -A -i ~/.ssh/hdm"

The public / private key-pair hdm was used during the exercise period. Since multiple key-pairs were available on the host system, an alias was created to make connecting to the Hetzner instances easier. The flag -i passes the specified private key file which will be used to authenticate against the server, while -A enables ssh-agent forwarding.

docs.title: VCI
docs.text:
alias vci='check-jsonschema --schemafile https://raw.githubusercontent.com/canonical/cloud-init/main/cloudinit/config/schemas/schema-cloud-config-v1.json'

Short for validate cloud-init, this alias was used to shorten the call to a third-party validation utility. Since the cloud-init package is not available for the system used during course work, the official JSON schema by Canonical was used to validate yaml configurations via check-jsonschema.

docs.title: Init script (init.sh)
docs.text:
The script inits.sh was written to facilitate easy module creation. It creates an exercise directory, copies the top level .env file and template Terraform code, and runs terraform init in the newly created directory: 

.
├── README.md
├── mkdocs
└── Terraform
    ├── init.sh
    └── ...

docs.title: Apply script (apply.sh)
docs.text:
A script to prepare the shell and call terraform apply is provided in the Terraform directory:

.
├── README.md
├── mkdocs
└── Terraform
    ├── apply.sh
    └── ...

It can be called with any exercise number as a command line argument. The script will source the .env file in the directory of the provided exercise number and call both terraform init and terraform apply from inside the directory.

The script was written to make the exercise results easily reproducible from the course work home directory (Terraform).

docs.title: Templates and Modules
docs.text:
Templates can be found in the Templates directory:

.
├── README.md
├── mkdocs
└── Terraform
    ├── Templates
    └── Modules
    └── ...

Different modules have been created in the Modules directory, which provide outputs that are used throughout the project. To learn more, visit:

  • HashiCorp - Modules
  • HashiCorp - Outputs

If you elect not to use the init.sh script when creating a new module for an exercise, you need to manually copy the template files into the exercise directory and remove the .template suffix.

docs.title: .env.template
docs.text:
This template contains the environment variables which are used throughout many solutions. Copy the template into the desired exercise directory and change the contents to contain your secrets. Rename the file to .env and source it to reproduce the documented results.

To learn more, visit:

  • Dotenv
  • The Linux Documentation Project - Sourcing a file

docs.title: Conf
docs.text:
The file Modules/Config/config.tf contains commonly used values, including SSH-keys of authorized users for the servers created when running the exercise solutions. Update config.tf.template with your desired values and rename it to config.tf.

If you wish to add an SSH-key, it is sufficient to add it to the authorizedKeys output directive, it will be applied to all exercise solutions using it:

output "authorizedKeys" {
  description = "List of authorized users' public ssh keys"
  type        = map(string)
  value = { ADD YOUR SSH KEYS HERE }
}

To learn how to utilize maps, visit:

  • HashiCorp - Terraform Types and Values

You may change the username for authorized users on the servers. The default value is devops:

output "loginUserName" {
  description = "Login user's name with admin privileges"
  type        = string
  value       = "devops"
}

To execute generated shell script from any location on your file system, the exercises create them in a user specified directory. You may supply a bin directory, or any directory on your $PATH:

output "bin" {
  description = "Local user bin directory"
  type = string
  value = ADD YOUR bin DIRECTORY OR ANY DIRECTORY ON YOUR PATH HERE (ensure terraform can write to the directory)
}

Note:

If you wish to chose a location for the scripts that isn't known via $PATH, take care to invoke the scripts like you would any regular shell script (./).

To learn more, visit;

  • The Linux Documentation Project - PATH
  • The Linux Foundation - /bin

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
The file Modules/Firewall/firewall.tf contains common firewall rules, which can be added to the dynamic rule creation present in Templates/firewall.tf.template:

resource "hcloud_firewall" "TEMPLATE" {
  name = "TEMPLATE"

  dynamic "rule" {
    for_each = {
      for name in [TEMPLATE_ADD_RULE_NAMES_HERE] : name => module.firewall.firewall_rules[name]
    }
    content {
      description = rule.value.description
      direction   = rule.value.direction
      protocol    = rule.value.protocol
      port        = rule.value.port
      source_ips  = rule.value.source_ips
    }
  }
}

To learn more, visit:

  • Terraform Registry - hcloud_firewall
  • HashiCorp - Dynamic Blocks

One example of a common firewall rule (SSH-Traffic via 22) inside firewall.tf.template:

locals {
  firewall_rules = {
    ssh = {
      description = "Allow SSH"
      direction   = "in"
      protocol    = "tcp"
      port        = "2222"
      source_ips  = ["0.0.0.0/0", "::/0"]
    }
    ...

To learn more, visit:

  • HashiCorp - Locals

These rules are accessible via the modules output directive:

output "firewall_rules" {
  description = "Reusable firewall rule definitions"
  value       = local.firewall_rules
}

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
The file Modules/Server/server.tf contains common server attributes, which can be added to the server resource present in Templates/main.tf.template:

resource "hcloud_server" "g01" {
  name         = module.server.serverName_g01
  image        = module.server.serverImage
  server_type  = module.server.serverType
  location     = module.server.serverLocation
  ssh_keys     = [for key in hcloud_ssh_key.sshKeys : key.id]
}

To learn more, visit:

-Terraform Registry - hcloud_server

These default values are accessible via the modules output directive, of which this is one example:

output "serverType" {
  description = "The cheapest server Type (cx23)"
  value = "cx23"
}

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: This section chronicles common issues encountered while working on the submissions that are too general to explain in any given solution.

docs.title: Server Type
docs.text:
Every exercise solution that requires server creation uses the cheapest Hetzner server type cx23. These servers are not selectable via the GUI, but can still be created via the API. It can happen that all servers of this type are unavailable, in which case terrraform apply will produce the error:

resource unavailable

If this were to happen, you may elect to switch to a more expensive server type like cx02 to continue examining the provided solutions.

docs.title: Operating System Differences
docs.text: Solutions were produced on OS X. Operating System differences may lead to solutions not working right out of the box without adjustments.

docs.title: File Paths
docs.text: If file paths seem to be incorrect, check if your operating system expects different characters delineating inodes or if escape sequences differ.

docs.title: Dependency Lock Files
docs.text:
Lock files have been committed to version control, since they contain the provider versions used when the exercise solutions were submitted. This was done to document with which version solutions were functional, in case a later release breaks the provided source code. If you are using a different operating system or are installing providers from a custom source, the lock files may cause problems.

The lock files have been populated with checksums for multiple major operating system versions. If you still encounter problems check if your operating system was omitted:

terraform providers lock \
  -platform=windows_amd64 \
  -platform=windows_arm64
  -platform=linux_amd64 \
  -platform=linux_arm64 \
  -platform=darwin_amd64 \
  -platform=darwin_arm64

If you wish to run the submitted code with the most recent available provider versions, run terraform init -upgrade.

To read more, visit:

  • HashiCorp - Dependency Lock Files
  • HashiCorp - terraform providers lock command

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: If shell scripts aren't executable after cloning the repository, check and set the execution permissions for your user. When writing files to directories (like e.g. /usr/bin), ensure these directories can be written to.

docs.title: Task
docs.text: No. 19 Cloud-init for starters

docs.title: Cloud-init for starters
docs.text: Follow Hetzner's Cloud-init introduction and assemble a corresponding cloud-init script. Use the package_reboot_if_required: true directive in favor of an explicit reboot command. Use the Hetzner WEB Gui for manual server creation. Copy-paste your cloud-init script into the respective text field.

docs.title: Hetzner - Basic Cloud Config
docs.text: Summary of Hetzner's Cloud-init introduction.

docs.title: Step 1 - Insert first line
docs.text:
The cloud-init config uses YAML ("YAML Ain't Markup Language") as markup language. The file must start with a comment on the first line so that the code is interpreted as cloud-config by the server:

#cloud config

docs.title: Step 2 - Create user
docs.text: After the initial comment, let us start by creating a new admin user with sudo privileges and pre-configured SSH key.

docs.title: Step 3 - Update packages
docs.text: The first thing we do is an update of the package lists and installed packages. A fresh copy of Linux may have outdated packages with critical security vulnerabilities. In this step, you could install necessary packages for your projects too.

docs.title: Step 4 – Harden SSH
docs.text: We need to create a new file in sshd_config.d. Settings in /etc/ssh/sshd_config are automatically overwritten by any *.conf file within the sshd_config.d directory. - Deactivate the root login - Enable user for SSH - Change the default port for SSH - Deactivate password authentication - Automatic disconnection in case of incorrect login - Deactivate unused functions

docs.title: Step 5.1 - Configure fail2ban
docs.text: To secure the SSH network protocol, use fail2ban against brute force attacks

docs.title: Step 5.2 – Enable ufw
docs.text: Make sure you allow the respective SSH port.

docs.title: Step 6 – Create the server
docs.text: Open the Hetzner Console, select your project and create a server. In the "Cloud config" text box, enter the configuration you just created.

docs.title: Cloud-init configuration
docs.text:
To create the configuration, follow the instructions laid out in Hetzner - Basic Cloud Config. The page provides the full configuration necessary to create the basic server instance via cloud-init.

Cloud-init generates its own config file 50-cloud-init.conf automatically, which enables password login by default:

To ensure the desired SSH configuration takes effect, an additional parameter has to be added to prevent password login from being enabled:

ssh_pwauth: false

docs.title: Verifying the configuration
docs.text: To verify the configuration was created correctly, run the schema validation:

docs.title: Server creation
docs.text:
To create the server, log into the Hetzner Console, select a project, and navigate to the Servers tab in the sidebar.

There a server can be bought and created manually. Paste the cloud-init configuration in the Cloud config text box and buy the server.

Note: No SSH keys were provided manually, since the configuration will add them to authorized_keys automatically.

docs.title: Logging into the server
docs.text:
After waiting for the script to run, log into the newly created server. Since we changed the port SSH runs on, we have to specify -p 2222:

ssh -i ~/.ssh/hdm -p 2222 holu@167.233.84.111

Note that a login as user root is no longer possible:

Logging in has to be done as the user holu:

Attempting a login without a permitted public key fails without allowing password login:

Logging in was successful, confirming the cloud-init configuration was loaded. The specified SSH keys were placed into the server's authorized_keys file:

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
The configuration was supposed to set up a simple firewall, allowing only incoming SSH traffic to establish a connection.

The firewall created via cloud-init drops all packets except SSH traffic. ICMP is usually enabled by default if a server is created via the Hetzner GUI, but pinging the server for example doesn't work anymore since the firewall rules don't allow them through:

docs.title: Fail2Ban
docs.text:
In addition, fail2ban was set up. Repeated failed attempts are already penalized by the system, meaning fail2ban doesn't register the unsuccessful tries:

It is possible to confirm the tool was still set up by checking the service status:

docs.title: Task
docs.text: No. 20 Cloud-init by Terraform

docs.title: Cloud-init by Terraform
docs.text: Re-use your Cloud-init script from Cloud-init for starters. This time follow Figure 1106, “Terraform triggering Cloud-init” using Terraform for executing Cloud-init rather than Hetzner's WEB GUI.

docs.title: Server creation with Terraform
docs.text:
To avoid having to create the server manually, server creation via Terraform was set up.

Run the following command in the directory 20. Cloud-init by Terraform or execute the apply.sh script with the command line argument 20 to create the server via Terraform.

terraform init && terraform apply

docs.title: Cloud provider
docs.text:
To be able to access the Hetzner API, the hcloud cloud provider needs to be initialized:

terraform {
  required_providers {
    hcloud = {
      source = "hetznercloud/hcloud"
    }
  }
  required_version = ">= 0.13"
}

hcloud: The provider hetznercloud/hcloud allows interfacing with Hetzner's infrastructure via Terraform. To learn more, visit: - Terraform Registry - Hetzner Cloud Provider

docs.title: Hetzner Cloud API token
docs.text:
To be able to purchase a server instance, the generated API token (as per Prerequisites) has to be read from the shell environment:

provider "hcloud" {
token = var.hcloud_token
}

To be able to source the token from a confidential .env file, follow the instructions in the Templates preliminary. Alternatively, you can export the secret directly to be stored as an environment variable in your current shell session:

export TF_VAR_hcloud_token=YOUR_TOKEN_HERE

To learn more, visit: The Linux Documentation Project - Bash Variables

docs.title: Server creation
docs.text:
# Create the server
resource "hcloud_server" "g01" {
  name         = "g01"
  image        = var.serverImage
  server_type  = var.serverType
  location     = "nbg1"

  # Post server creation init script
  user_data    = file("cloud-init.yaml")
}

To read more about server resource creation, visit:

  • Terraform - Resources
  • Terraform Registry - hcloud_server

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Commonly used values have been stored in variables for ease of access:

variable "hcloud_token" {
  description = "Hetzner API token"
  type = string
  nullable = false
  sensitive = true
}

variable "serverImage" {
  description = "Server image"
  type = string
  nullable = true
  default = "debian-13"
}

variable "serverType" {
  description = "Server type"
  type = string
  nullable = true
  default = "cx23"
}

To learn more about Terraform variables, visit: Terraform - Variables

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
To be able to connect to the server immediately after the init-script has finished, an output directive was added in the file output.tf. It outputs the IPv4 address the server was assigned:

output "ip" {
  value = hcloud_server.g01.ipv4_address
}

To learn more about Terraform output, visit: Terraform - Output

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
The resulting server configuration was the same as described in Exercise 19. Results, except for the following:

  • A cheaper server type was selectable via the API, meaning the server ran on a machine with fewer resources.

Terraform allows creation of the server type Cost-Optimized CX23:

variable "serverType" {
  description = "Server type"
  type = string
  nullable = true
  default = "cx23"
}

Servers of type CX23 are only available in limited amounts and sometimes not selectable via the GUI:

  • The deployment was now possible via Terraform, meaning the need for manual GUI interaction was gone.

This means the deployment can be done via shell and therefore automated:

docs.title: Task
docs.text: No. 21 - Enhancing index.html generation

docs.title: Enhancing index.html generation
docs.text:
We extend our exercise Cloud-init by Terraform: - We recently cheated by creating an invalid HTML file:

echo "I'm Nginx @ $(curl -4 https://ifconfig.me) created $(date -u)" > /var/www/html/index.html

This time start from a proper tpl/index.html template file:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>Template demo</title>
  </head>
  <body>                                     <!-- To become e.g. Sunday 08 Nov 2026 at 18:08 --->
    <h1>Terraform template file demo created ${creationDate}.</h1> 
    <p>This is server <b>${serverName}</b> having IP addresses:</p>
     <ul>
       <li>IPV4: <a href="http://${ipv4Address}">${ipv4Address}</a></li>          <!-- To become e.g. 2a01:4f8:c016:9b2::/64 -->
       <li>IPV6: <a href="http://[${ipv6Address}]">${ipv6Address}</a> from subnet ${ipv6Subnet}</li>
     </ul>
  </body>
</html>
  • Use Terraform's templatefile(...) function to replace all five variables by their respective values using Terraform for generating a gen/index.html file.
  • Use Cloud-init to transfer the generated index.html file to its respective location on your destination server. Nginx should then be happily picking it up.

docs.title: Setup (setup.tf)
docs.text: The project was created via the init.sh script, which created the base directory and the setup.tf file: Assume this script was run to create the following exercises. If anything was altered or omitted, the setup section of that exercise's solution page will specify which steps were taken.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
This file contains the base components used across many exercises, such as the required providers:

terraform {
  required_providers {
    hcloud = ...
    local = {
      source = "hashicorp/local"
    }
  }
  required_version = ">= 1.5"
}

In addition to the hcloud provider (see Ex. 19. Cloud-init for starters/1. Solution), the provider for local file interfacing is necessary:

local: The local provider by Hashicorp enables use of functions that operate on the local file system. To lean more, visit: - Terraform Registry - Hashicorp Local Provider

docs.title: Api Token
docs.text: The API token was created in the same manner as it was in Ex. 19. Cloud-init for starters/1. Solution.

docs.title: SSH Keys
docs.text:
The SSH keys allowed to access the server were imported via setup.tf.template:

# Load the common configuration
module "config" {
  source = "../Modules/Conf"
}

# Set up SSH keys
resource "hcloud_ssh_key" "sshKeys" {
  for_each   = module.config.authorizedKeys
  name       = each.key
  public_key = each.value
}

To learn more, visit:

  • Terraform Registry - hcloud_ssh_keys Resource

docs.title: index.html
docs.text:
The index.html template from the exercise description was copied into the directory 21. Enhancing index.html generation/templates. It contains the following interpolation sequences for which values will be provided later:

- ${creationDate}
- ${serverName}
- ${ipv4Address}
- ${ipv6Address}
- ${ipv6Subnet}

These sequences will be replaced by the templatefile function.

To learn more, visit:

  • Hashicorp - templatefile function

docs.title: cloud-init.yaml
docs.text:
The cloud-init.yaml template was created in the directory 21. Enhancing index.html generation/templates. The configuration was written in HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language) beforehand and then wrapped in a call to ${yamlencode(). This was done to prevent indentation problems which can occur during string interpolation. To learn more, visit:

  • HashiCorp - yamlencode
  • HashiCorp - Terraform language types and values

To enable our webserver to access the dynamically generated index.html file, we need to copy it into the /var/www/html directory. We also set permission so the file can be read by the reverse proxy we will use to serve the content (nginx).

write_files = [
  {
    content     = "${html}"
    path        = "/var/www/html/index.html"
    permissions = "0644"
    owner       = "root:root"
  }
]

To learn more, visit:

  • Cloud-init - Write files
  • Linux Foundation - File permissions

All that was left to do is write the instructions for the webserver to be installed and run:

packages = ["nginx"]
runcmd = [
    "systemctl enable nginx",
    "systemctl start nginx"
  ]

docs.title: Network configuration
docs.text:
The webpage is supposed to display the webserver's IP addresses, which requires us to create a resource for each IP type:

resource "hcloud_primary_ip" "ipv4" {
  name        = "primary-ipv4"
  location    = module.server.serverLocation
  type        = "ipv4"
  auto_delete = true
}

resource "hcloud_primary_ip" "ipv6" {
  name        = "primary-ipv6"
  location    = module.server.serverLocation
  type        = "ipv6"
  auto_delete = true
}

It is important to provide both resources with the same location, since the IPs need to be located in the same datacenter for the server creation to work. We set auto_delete to true. The IP addresses will be deleted by Hetzner once the servers no longer exist (i.e. you call terraform destroy).

To learn more, visit:

  • Terraform registry - hcloud_primary_ip

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
To allow web traffic, we need to allow inbound HTTP traffic. Additionally, set up SSH access and whitelist ICMP packets for easier server access and simpler monitoring. Add the names "ssh", "icmp", "http" to the list of common firewall rules inside the firewall resource created by the init.sh script:

for name in ["ssh", "icmp", "http"] : name => module.firewall.firewall_rules[name]

docs.title: index.html
docs.text:
To create the static webpage nginx should serve under the server's IP the file needs to generated by interpolating the strings listed in Templates - index.html This can be achieved via the previously mentioned templatefile function. It can replace content in a local file and save the generated output.

The function takes as many arguments as should be replaced as a key-value pair. It matches the provided keys against strings to be interpolated and replaces them with the associated value. We need to pass the attributes of the previously created IP resources to this function to replace the placeholders in the template. This needs to happen after resource creation of the IPs, since the ouput will be a static html file which requires the values to be hard-coded in.

resource "local_file" "index" {
  content = templatefile("templates/index.html", {
    creationDate = timestamp()
    serverName   = module.server.serverName_g01
    ipv4Address  = hcloud_primary_ip.ipv4.ip_address
    ipv6Address  = hcloud_primary_ip.ipv6.ip_address
    ipv6Subnet   = hcloud_primary_ip.ipv6.ip_network
  })
  filename = "gen/index.html"
}

The generated output will be saved to gen/index.htlm:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <title>Template demo</title>
</head>
<body>
<h1>Terraform template file demo created 2026-11-10T12:10:43Z.</h1>
<p>This is server <b>g01</b> with IP addresses:</p>
<ul>
    <li>IPV4: <a href="http://2.31.146.28">2.31.146.28</a></li>
    <li>IPV6: <a href="http://[2a01:4f8:1c1c:bbd6::]">2a01:4f8:1c1c:bbd6::</a> from subnet 2a01:4f8:1c1c:bbd6::/64</li>
</ul>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: cloud-init.yaml
docs.text:
The generated html file can now be passed into our cloud-init config. We need to provide the parameter html with the previously generated file accessible via local_file to interpolate "${html}".

resource "local_file" "cloud-init" {
  content = templatefile("templates/cloud-init.yaml", {
    html = local_file.index.content
  })
  filename = "gen/cloud-init.yaml"
}

The generated output will be saved to gen/cloud-init.yaml:

#cloud-config

"packages":
- "nginx"
"runcmd":
- "systemctl enable nginx"
- "systemctl start nginx"
"write_files":
- "content": |-
    <!DOCTYPE html>
    <html lang="en">
    <head>
        <title>Template demo</title>
    </head>
    <body>
    <h1>Terraform template file demo created 2026-11-10T12:10:43Z.</h1>
    <p>This is server <b>g01</b> with IP addresses:</p>
    <ul>
        <li>IPV4: <a href="http://2.31.146.28">2.31.146.28</a></li>
        <li>IPV6: <a href="http://[2a01:4f8:1c1c:bbd6::]">2a01:4f8:1c1c:bbd6::</a> from subnet 2a01:4f8:1c1c:bbd6::/64</li>
    </ul>
    </body>
    </html>
  "owner": "root:root"
  "path": "/var/www/html/index.html"
  "permissions": "0644"

docs.title: Verifying the output
docs.text:
To verify the generated cloud-init.yaml file, we can target the local file creation explicitly without creating the server resource. Supply the option -target=local_file.cloud-init when running terraform apply. This will only execute the resource creation of the cloud-init file, as well as all other operations it depends on:

This confirms the file is correctly encoded.

Note:

This already creates the IPs on Hetzner's end, since the cloud-init creation depends on the index.html creation, which in turn depends on the IP address resources. Run terraform destroy after this step!

docs.title: Server Creation
docs.text:
To use the common server parameters, load the server module:

module "server" {
  source = "../Modules/Server"
}

We then instantiate the server resource with the common parameters and resources, as well as the IP addresses and cloud-init configuration we created in the previous steps.

resource "hcloud_server" "g01" {
  name         = module.server.serverName_g01
  image        = module.server.serverImage
  server_type  = module.server.serverType
  location     = module.server.serverLocation
  ssh_keys     = [for key in hcloud_ssh_key.sshKeys : key.id]
  firewall_ids = [hcloud_firewall.nginx.id]

  public_net {
    ipv4 = hcloud_primary_ip.ipv4.id
    ipv6 = hcloud_primary_ip.ipv6.id
  }

  user_data = local_file.cloud-init.content
}

To learn more, visit:

  • Terraform Registry - hcloud_server Primary IPs

Note:

The combination of the default server type cx23 and the default location nbg1 might not be available. If this occurs, you can try another location (e.g. fsn1). Keep in mind, the location declared in the IP resources must be changed accordingly!

docs.text: Logging in as root via SSH was possible as intended:

docs.text: No. 22 - Hardening your server

docs.title: Hardening your server
docs.text:
Extending the previous exercise we address login and firewall related issues.

  1. Define a hcloud_firewall in favor of a server local ufw allowing only ssh access. You should not be able to access your server using http://\<serverIP>

  2. Add port 80 to the list of allowed incoming connections. Your server should become accessible.

  3. With respect to Figure 1113, “Watch out for your enemies! ” inspect the output of journalctl -f on your server for a while. Can you spot suspicious login attempts?

Read the sshd_config(5) - Linux man page. Then provide a configuration file /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99Local.conf by using Cloud-init again. Use this file for overriding suitable ssh server defaults:

  • Create a user devops eligible for both ssh login and sudo execution.

    Then restrict ssh logins to the devops user account thereby excluding all other users.

  • Disallow ssh password authentication altogether

On success the following sequence should be possible:

$ ssh -v devops@95.217.154.104
...
debug1: SSH2_MSG_SERVICE_ACCEPT received
debug1: Authentications that can continue: publickey ❶
debug1: Next authentication method: publickey
...
Last login: Sun May  5 19:21:12 2024 from 217.245.243.187

devops@hello:~$ sudo su - ❷
root@hello:~# hostname
hello

  • password is not among the list of allowed authentication methods.

  • User devops may execute sudo commands by virtue of his membership in the sudo group .

On contrary without owning an authorized private key ssh root or devops logins must be prohibited:

$ ssh root@95.217.154.104
root@95.217.154.104: Permission denied (publickey).

$ ssh devops@95.217.154.104
devops@95.217.154.104: Permission denied (publickey).

Read the cloud-init documentation and/or related tutorials to:

  • Currently, your (most likely outdated) cloud provider supplied distribution does not get upgraded on installation time:
$ ./bin/ssh
...
devops@hello:~$ sudo su -
root@hello:~# apt update
Hit:1 http://security.debian.org/debian-security bookworm-security InRelease
Hit:2 http://deb.debian.org/debian bookworm InRelease                                              
...
Reading package lists... Done
Building dependency tree... Done
Reading state information... Done
6 packages can be upgraded. Run 'apt list --upgradable' to see them.

# apt list --upgradable
Listing... Done
less/stable-security,stable-security 590-2.1~deb12u2 amd64 [upgradable from: 590-2]
libc-bin/stable-security,stable-security 2.36-9+deb12u7 amd64 [upgradable from: 2.36-9+deb12u6]

locales/stable-security,stable-security 2.36-9+deb12u7 all [upgradable from: 2.36-9+deb12u6]
Modify your Cloud-init configuration to upgrade your distribution at server creation time. If so required your system should also reboot.

  • Install and configure fail2ban limiting ssh failed connection attempts.

  • Install the plocate file indexer package and initialize it.

On success all packages should be up to date:

$ ./bin/ssh
...
devops@hello:~$ sudo su -
root@hello:~# apt update
Hit:1 http://security.debian.org/debian-security bookworm-security InRelease

All packages are up to date.

Failed login attempts should be banned: Keep a second login open in advance when trying to simulate login failures! You should then see a report similar to:

root@hello:~# fail2ban-client status sshd

|- Filter
|  |- Currently failed: 2
|  |- Total failed: 14
|  `- Journal matches:  _SYSTEMD_UNIT=sshd.service + _COMM=sshd
`- Actions

Searching for file name components should work like e.g.:

/etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
Supplying a firewall that only allows SSH traffic can be achieved by supplying only the rule name ssh in the file firewall.tf:

for name in ["ssh"] : name => module.firewall.firewall_rules[name]

To allow web traffic, the same setup already applied in Ex. 21 - Working on Cloud-init was used.

docs.title: Upgrading the server automatically
docs.text:
To upgrade the distribution at server creation time, the following directives can be added to the cloud-init configuration:

package_reboot_if_required: true
package_update: true
package_upgrade: true

The package_reboot_if_required directive ensures that the system reboots if necessary to complete the operation.

docs.title: Installing and running services
docs.text:
The exercise calls for three services, nginx, fail2ban, and plocate. To install them, add their respective name to the packages directive, and enable it with systemctl under the run-cmd directive:

packages:
  - nginx
  - fail2ban
  - plocate

runcmd:
  - systemctl enable fail2ban
  - systemctl enable nginx
  - systemctl enable plocate
  - sudo updatedb

docs.title: Plocate
docs.text:
plocate additionally requires sudo updatedb to initialize the index-based locate command. To learn more, visit:

  • plocate

docs.title: Devops user
docs.text:
To set up the user devops, cloud-init was employed. Add the following line to assign sudo rights to the user devops:

sudo: ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL

The complete user configuration should look like this:

users:
  - name: devops
    groups: users, admin
    sudo: ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL
    shell: /bin/bash
    ssh_authorized_keys:
      - YOUR PUBLIC KEYS HERE

Dynamic user creation will be done in the next exercise, see Ex. 23 - Solving the known_hosts quirk

docs.title: SSHD Configuration
docs.text:
To alter the default ssh daemon configuration, cloud-init was employed to write a configuration file to /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/. Both root login and authentication via password were disabled via PermitRootLogin no and PasswordAuthentication no respectively.

write_files:
  - path: /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99Local.conf
    content: |
      PermitRootLogin no
      PasswordAuthentication no
      AllowUsers devops

To learn more, visit:

  • sshd_config(5) - Linux man page

docs.text: Ex. 23 - Solving the ~/.ssh/known_hosts quirk

docs.title: Solving the ~/.ssh/known_hosts quirk
docs.text:
Extend Hardening your server generating both a bin/ssh wrapper and a corresponding gen/known_hosts file to be used by the wrapper script.

Avoiding ssh host key issues on login we require the creation of a known_hosts file among with each server being created:

157.180.78.16 ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIJDd+x7b80BM97rTU4RCM/CP+K7u4QAqx8ulDdXm9JDv We assume this file being generated at gen/known_hosts. A corresponding ssh bash script shall be generated at the same level in bin/ssh:

docs.title: !/bin/bash
docs.text:
GEN_DIR=$(dirname "$0")/../gen

ssh -o UserKnownHostsFile="$GEN_DIR/known_hosts" devops@157.180.78.16 "$@"

docs.title: end of script
docs.text:
This way invoking ./bin/ssh will instruct the ssh client to read gen/known_hosts and thus avoiding unknown host key issues. The "$@" allows for optional user provided parameters.

For generating this script we start from a corresponding tpl/ssh.sh template file:

docs.title: !/usr/bin/env bash
docs.text:
GEN_DIR=$(dirname "$0")/../gen

ssh -o UserKnownHostsFile="$GEN_DIR/known_hosts" ${devopsUsername}@${ip} "$@"

docs.title: end of script
docs.text:
We then let Terraform use this template replacing ${devopsUsername} and ${ip} by your deployment's actual values.

As shown in Figure 1132, “Parent module vs. sub module context ” point to your child module's local tpl path by using ${path.module}:

resource "local_file" "ssh_script" { content = templatefile("${path.module}/tpl/ssh.sh", { ... } Likewise create a bin/scp script to be used for file transfer purposes as well:

docs.title: !/usr/bin/env bash
docs.text:
GEN_DIR=$(dirname "$0")/../gen

if [ $# -lt 2 ]; then echo usage: .../bin/scp ... devops@157.180.78.16 ... else scp -o UserKnownHostsFile="$GEN_DIR/known_hosts" $@ fi

docs.title: end of script
docs.text: Since copying objects requires at least a source and a destination parameter this script checks for the presence of at least two extra user supplied values by means of if [ $# -lt 2 ].

docs.title: Generating a key-pair for the server
docs.text:
Fingerprinting detection can trip if a server has the same IP address as an already known instance. This happens because a newly created key-pair is now associated with an IP address for a known host with an originally different SSH key. A known key-pair should be placed on the server to remedy this problem.

To create a key-pair for the server, a tls_private_key resource needs to be created:

resource "tls_private_key" "host" { algorithm = "ED25519" }

To learn more, visit:

  • Terraform Registry - tls_private_key

docs.title: User data
docs.text:
To be able to pass user_data to the server, a local file needs to be created. Use the templatefile function to that end. It can accept values dynamically, therefore it can supply the server with the previously created SSH key-pair. Use it to configure the SSH rules as well.

To configure the cloud-init configuration, a template file is needed. Use templates/userData.yaml. It contains the update and upgrade directives for the system's packages already covered in previous exercises.

Additionally, it configures the SSH daemon to disallow password and root login, which has already been covered as well. One change to make is introducing a template string for the user to dynamically configure the username of the admin account:

write_files:
  - path: /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99Local.conf
    content: |
      PermitRootLogin no
      PasswordAuthentication no
      AllowUsers ${devopsUsername}

The template string can be used to define the users directive as well. Authorized SSH keys can be passed into the configuration with interpolation dynamically as well. The ssh_authorized_keys placeholder should be replaced with a map of string, which should contain the desired SSH keys as values. These values can be accessed via the values function:

${yamlencode({
users = [
{
name                = devopsUsername
groups              = ["users", "admin"]
sudo                = "ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL"
shell               = "/bin/bash"
ssh_authorized_keys = values(ssh_authorized_keys)
}
]

Now the SSH keys for the server can be defined and encoded via yamlencode as well. Add a placeholder for both public (host_ed25519_public) and private (host_ed25519_private) keys:

  ssh_keys = {
  ed25519_private = host_ed25519_private
  ed25519_public  = host_ed25519_public
  }

The resource should provide values for all placeholders so they can be interpolated correctly when generating the output. Place the output in a generated file directory (e.g. gen) via the filename key. Pass the content through the templatefile function, and provide the variable values which should be interpolated. Use the generated tls_private_key for host_ed25519_public and host_ed25519_private. Pass the desired loginUserName (e.g. the default user devops from the config.tf.template file), and the desired SSH public keys which should be authorized to log in as that user.

resource "local_file" "user_data" {
  filename = "${path.module}/gen/user_data.yaml"
  content = templatefile("${path.module}/templates/userData.yaml", {
    host_ed25519_private = tls_private_key.host.private_key_openssh
    host_ed25519_public  = tls_private_key.host.public_key_openssh
    devopsUsername       = module.config.loginUserName
    ssh_authorized_keys  = module.config.authorizedKeys
  })
  depends_on = [tls_private_key.host]
}

docs.title: Server creation
docs.text:
You may create the default server as it is defined in Templates/main.tf.template now. Add the following line to pass the previously created cloud-init configuration:

user_data = local_file.user_data.content

It should look like the following:

resource "hcloud_server" "g01" {
  name        = module.server.serverName_g01
  image       = module.server.serverImage
  server_type = module.server.serverType
  location    = module.server.serverLocation

  ssh_keys  = [for key in hcloud_ssh_key.sshKeys : key.id]
  firewall_ids = [hcloud_firewall.SSH.id]
  user_data = local_file.user_data.content

  depends_on = [local_file.user_data]
}

docs.title: Known Hosts
docs.text:
To be able to pass the generated key-pair as a known host for the IP the server was just created with, a known_hosts file has to be created. Combine the server's ipv4_address with the tls_private_key to form the contents of the file. Place the generated file in your gen directory and set the appropriate permissions.

resource "local_file" "known_hosts" {
  content = join(" ",
    [hcloud_server.g01.ipv4_address, tls_private_key.host.public_key_openssh]
  )
  filename        = "${path.module}/gen/known_hosts"
  file_permission = "644"
  depends_on      = [hcloud_server.g01]
}

docs.title: SSH wrappers
docs.text: The wrapper scripts can now be created to facilitate easier interfacing with the server via SSH.

docs.title: SSH wrapper
docs.text:
Use the template templates/ssh.sh as a base for the generated wrapper. It calls scp with the generated known_hosts file, preventing the detection of changed SSH keys without having to alter the system's base known_hosts file.

#!/bin/bash
ssh -i "${pk}" -o "UserKnownHostsFile=\"${genDir}/known_hosts\"" devops@${ip} "$@"

Interpolate the variables via the templatefile function. Pass the server's IP address via the ip variable. Pass the path to your private key file via the pk variable. Pass the absolute path of your gen directory via the genDir variable.

Save the generated script to your bin directory (or any other directory set in $PATH) to be able to execute it from any arbitrary working directory. You may set the bin directory via the bin output directive in Modules/Conf/config.tf.template. Set the file permissions accordingly via file_permission:

resource "local_file" "ssh_script" {
  content = templatefile("${path.module}/templates/ssh.sh", {
    ip     = hcloud_server.g01.ipv4_address
    pk     = module.config.pk
    genDir = "${abspath(path.module)}/gen"
  })
  filename        = "${module.config.bin}/ssh${hcloud_server.g01.name}"
  file_permission = "755"
  depends_on      = [local_file.known_hosts]
}

The script can now be called via the concatenated strings ssh ad the server name.

docs.title: SCP wrapper
docs.text:
The script takes two parameters, which are the positional parameters taken by scp. It checks for their existence via $# -lt 2 to ensure the command is being invoked correctly, but it doesn't check if the parameter contents are valid. The script the calls scp with the generated known_hosts file, to the same end as the ssh wrapper does.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
if [ $# -lt 2 ]; then
   echo "usage: .../bin/scp ... devops@${ip} ..."
else
   scp -i "${pk}" -o "UserKnownHostsFile=\"${genDir}/known_hosts\"" "$@"
fi

SCP wrapper generation works in the exact same manner as it did for the SSH wrapper:

resource "local_file" "scp_script" {
  content = templatefile("${path.module}/templates/scp.sh", {
    ip     = hcloud_server.g01.ipv4_address
    pk     = module.config.pk
    genDir = "${abspath(path.module)}/gen"
  })
  filename        = "${module.config.bin}/scp${hcloud_server.g01.name}"
  file_permission = "755"
  depends_on      = [local_file.known_hosts]
}

The script can be called via the concatenated strings scp ad the server name.
